options: Episodic attacks with normal breathing between
Episodic wheeze, worse at night or with triggers (dust, cold, exercise)
Chronic wheeze in a long-term smoker
Recent surgery, immobilisation, or long travel
Known heart failure, ischaemic heart disease, or hypertension
Black stools or overt GI bleeding
Attacks with fear, tingling around mouth/fingers, at rest
Constant regardless of activity or emotion

red_flags: SpO2 < 92% on room air or central cyanosis
Respiratory rate > 30/min, inability to speak in full sentences, or use of accessory muscles
Sudden dyspnoea with pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, or unilateral leg swelling
Silent chest in a wheezy patient (exhaustion — impending arrest)
Dyspnoea with hypotension, chest pain, or new confusion
Stridor or suspected upper airway obstruction
exam: Record respiratory rate, SpO2 on room air, pulse, BP, and temperature together
Watch the patient speak — count words per breath and look for accessory muscle use
Inspect for central cyanosis and finger clubbing
Estimate JVP — raised in heart failure and massive PE, flat in pure airway disease

Auscultate lungs: bilateral basal crackles (pulmonary oedema), focal crackles or bronchial breathing (pneumonia), diffuse wheeze (asthma/COPD), absent sounds with stony dullness (effusion), absent sounds with hyper-resonance (pneumothorax)
Percuss both lung fields comparing sides — dullness vs hyper-resonance localises effusion vs pneumothorax
Auscultate the heart for gallop rhythm (S3 of failure) and murmurs (valve disease driving failure)
Press for pitting oedema over both shins and check sacral oedema if bed-bound
Examine calves for unilateral swelling or tenderness (DVT as PE source)
Inspect conjunctivae and palmar creases for pallor (anaemia)
Check tracheal position — deviation suggests large effusion or tension pneumothorax

investigations.why: One film separates most of the list: pulmonary oedema and cardiomegaly (heart failure), consolidation (pneumonia), pleural effusion, pneumothorax, hyperinflation (COPD); usually normal in PE, anaemia, and anxiety

Atrial fibrillation or ischaemia points to a cardiac driver of failure; sinus tachycardia with S1Q3T3 or right-heart strain supports PE; normal ECG with normal film shifts weight to asthma, anaemia, or anxiety
Directly rules anaemia in or out as the cause; leukocytosis supports pneumonia; polycythaemia suggests chronic hypoxia of long-standing COPD

investigations.test: Peak expiratory flow (pre/post bronchodilator) or spirometry if available
investigations.why: Significant variability or reversibility rules in asthma; fixed obstruction in a smoker supports COPD; normal flow argues against airway disease as the explanation

investigations.test: Blood glucose, renal function and electrolytes
investigations.why: Renal function and potassium contextualise suspected heart failure and its severity; metabolic acidosis (e.g. uncontrolled diabetes) can present as unexplained tachypnoea mimicking a respiratory cause
Only when PE pre-test probability is LOW — negative then rules PE out; skip when probability is high and go to imaging

investigations.test: Echocardiography (or NT-proBNP where the lab offers it)
investigations.why: Confirms or excludes heart failure and valve disease when the film and exam are equivocal — reduced ejection fraction or significant valve lesion rules the cardiac limb in
Confirms and quantifies pleural effusion before any diagnostic tap and distinguishes effusion from consolidation when the X-ray is ambiguous
Second-line — if PE probability is high or D-dimer positive; definitive rule-in/rule-out for PE when first-line tests leave it standing
